Lower sun exposure and vitamin D levels are among the most studied hypotheses, though the relationship is complex and multifactorial.

text: Antiperspirants containing aluminum cause Alzheimer's disease and breast cancer. Scientific studies from the 1990s conclusively proved this, which is why Europe has banned aluminum in all personal care products.
explanation: False. The aluminum-Alzheimer's link has been extensively studied and not confirmed. The Alzheimer's Society and Alzheimer's Association state this has been thoroughly investigated without evidence of causation. Europe has not banned aluminum in personal care products. The breast cancer claim also lacks supporting evidence.

text: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) can now be cured in more than 95% of infected people using direct-acting antiviral medications taken for just 8–12 weeks, with minimal side effects — a major advance over previous interferon-based treatments.
explanation: Accurate. Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) like sofosbuvir/velpatasvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir achieve sustained virologic response (functional cure) in >95% of HCV patients. This represents a revolution over interferon regimens that had <50% cure rates and severe side effects.

text: The Wim Hof breathing method has been clinically proven to cure Lyme disease, fibromyalgia, HIV, and autoimmune conditions. Patients who practice this method no longer need any medications and become immune to all infections.
explanation: False. Wim Hof's methods have been studied and do show interesting immune modulation effects in healthy individuals. However, no clinical trials support using them to 'cure' Lyme disease, fibromyalgia, HIV, or autoimmune conditions, or to replace medications for these conditions.

text: Childhood pneumonia is the single largest infectious cause of death in children worldwide, killing approximately 700,000 children under 5 each year, mostly in low- and middle-income countries.
explanation: Accurate. UNICEF and WHO data confirm pneumonia causes ~700,000 child deaths under 5 annually — about 14% of all under-5 deaths. Most are preventable through pneumococcal and Hib vaccination, zinc supplementation, breastfeeding promotion, and improved access to antibiotics.

text: Reading in dim light permanently damages your eyes. Children who read under insufficient lighting will require much stronger glasses by adulthood because low light causes permanent microscopic tears in retinal cells.
explanation: False. Reading in dim light causes temporary eyestrain and fatigue, but no permanent damage. The American Academy of Ophthalmology states there is no evidence dim lighting causes structural eye damage. Myopia (nearsightedness) has complex genetic and environmental causes unrelated to lighting conditions.

text: The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly worsened global mental health. Rates of anxiety and depression increased by 25% worldwide in the first year of the pandemic, according to a WHO analysis of 193 studies.
explanation: Accurate. A 2022 WHO scientific brief, based on systematic review of 193 studies, found anxiety disorders increased 26% and depression 28% in the first year of COVID-19. The pandemic disrupted mental health services precisely when demand increased most.

text: Essential oils like oregano oil and tea tree oil, when taken internally in high doses, are more effective than antibiotics at treating bacterial infections with no risk of antibiotic resistance.
explanation: False. While essential oils have demonstrated antimicrobial properties in lab settings, human clinical trials do not support using them as antibiotic replacements. High-dose internal use can cause toxicity, liver damage, and seizures. They do not replace antibiotics for serious infections.

text: Blood pressure screening is recommended for all adults. Hypertension can usually be managed through lifestyle changes including salt reduction, the DASH diet, regular exercise, and — if needed — medication.
explanation: Accurate. AHA/ACC guidelines recommend regular blood pressure screening for all adults starting at 18. Lifestyle modification is first-line for Stage 1 hypertension. Evidence-based interventions can lower systolic BP by 5–15 mmHg and significantly reduce cardiovascular events.

text: Eating breakfast is the most important meal of the day and skipping it causes metabolic damage, increased obesity risk, and decreased academic performance in children. This is why all doctors recommend never skipping breakfast.
explanation: False. While some observational studies associate breakfast skipping with worse outcomes, randomized trials show no universal benefit from eating breakfast. Effects depend heavily on what is eaten and individual circumstances. Children's academic performance associations are confounded by socioeconomic factors.

text: Eye tests can detect early signs of conditions beyond vision problems, including diabetes (diabetic retinopathy), hypertension, multiple sclerosis, and even some brain tumors, through examination of the retina and optic nerve.
explanation: Accurate. Ophthalmoscopy can reveal retinal changes characteristic of diabetic retinopathy, hypertensive retinopathy, papilledema (suggesting raised intracranial pressure), and optic nerve changes associated with neurological conditions. Regular eye exams are therefore important beyond just assessing vision.

text: Mercury in fish is so dangerous that pregnant women and children should never eat any fish. All seafood is contaminated at levels that cause immediate neurological damage and eating even one serving of fish per week is equivalent to mercury poisoning.
explanation: False. While high-mercury fish (shark, swordfish, king mackerel) should be limited in pregnancy, the FDA recommends pregnant women eat 2–3 servings of low-mercury fish weekly. Omega-3 fatty acids in fish support fetal brain development. Blanket fish avoidance may be more harmful than low-mercury fish consumption.

text: BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations significantly increase lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Women with BRCA1 mutations have a 55–72% lifetime risk of breast cancer compared to ~12% in the general population.
explanation: Accurate. Meta-analyses of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carriers show 55–72% and 45–69% lifetime breast cancer risks respectively, compared to ~12% population risk. BRCA mutations also substantially elevate ovarian cancer risk. Genetic counseling and testing are recommended for those with family history.

text: Spending time in nature and green spaces is associated with reduced stress, improved mood, better immune function, and lower rates of depression and anxiety. Studies show even 20 minutes in a park reduces cortisol levels.
explanation: Accurate. Multiple studies confirm the mental and physical health benefits of nature exposure ('green prescriptions'). A 2019 study in Frontiers in Psychology found 20–30 minutes sitting or walking in nature produced the largest cortisol reduction. Japan's 'forest bathing' (Shinrin-yoku) is a clinically studied practice.

text: Doctors have quietly confirmed that ear candles (inserting a hollow candle in the ear and lighting it) effectively remove ear wax deep from the ear canal. ENT specialists use them in hospitals across Europe.
explanation: False. Multiple clinical studies found ear candles do not create negative pressure or remove earwax. They cause burns to the outer ear and face, eardrum perforations, and have caused fires. The FDA has warned against their use. ENT specialists do not use them.

text: The flu vaccine is reformulated every year because influenza viruses mutate rapidly through antigenic drift and shift. WHO's Global Influenza Surveillance Network monitors strains year-round to select the best-matched vaccine components.
explanation: Accurate. WHO's FluNet system tracks influenza strains globally, and twice yearly the WHO convenes experts to recommend vaccine compositions for the upcoming season in each hemisphere. Antigenic drift (gradual) and shift (sudden, pandemic-causing) drive the need for annual updates.

text: Herbal supplement companies are not required to prove their products work or are safe before selling them, because supplements are regulated differently than drugs in the United States under DSHEA (1994).
explanation: Accurate. The Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA) of 1994 means supplement manufacturers do not need FDA pre-approval or clinical trial evidence of efficacy or safety. They cannot claim to 'treat' diseases, but can make 'structure/function' claims.

text: Ancient Sumerian clay tablets show that doctors 5,000 years ago used the same pharmaceutical drugs we have today. This proves natural remedies from the ancient world are scientifically superior to modern medicine.
explanation: False. Ancient Sumerian medical texts do reference herbal treatments, but these bear no equivalence to modern pharmaceuticals, which are isolated, standardized compounds with clinical trial evidence. Some ancient plant remedies have led to drug discoveries (aspirin from willow bark), but ancient texts don't validate modern pharmaceutical equivalence.

text: Naloxone (Narcan) can rapidly reverse opioid overdose and is available without prescription in all U.S. states. Bystanders who administer it cannot be held legally liable for its use in a Good Samaritan emergency.
explanation: Accurate. The FDA approved over-the-counter naloxone nasal spray (Narcan) in 2023. All 50 U.S. states have enacted at least some form of naloxone access law, and most provide Good Samaritan protections for bystanders who respond to overdoses. Naloxone has saved hundreds of thousands of lives.

text: Spending more than 3 hours per day on social media is associated with significantly higher rates of depression, anxiety, loneliness, and body image issues in adolescents, particularly girls.
explanation: Accurate. Multiple prospective studies including those by Jean Twenge and Jonathan Haidt find robust associations between heavy social media use and depression/anxiety in teens, with stronger effects in girls. The mechanisms include social comparison, cyberbullying, sleep disruption, and reduced in-person interaction.

text: Laughing for 10 minutes per day has been scientifically proven to cure cancer by boosting natural killer cell activity by 400%. Oncologists recommend laughter therapy as a replacement for chemotherapy in early-stage cancer.
explanation: False. Laughter does have modest positive effects on mood, stress, and some immune parameters, but no evidence supports it curing cancer. No oncologist recommends laughter therapy as a cancer treatment replacement. The '400% NK cell boost cures cancer' claim is fabricated.

text: Measles can be fatal, particularly in malnourished children or those in low-income settings. The WHO estimates measles vaccination prevented 21.1 million deaths between 2000 and 2017.
explanation: Accurate. WHO data shows global measles deaths fell from 536,000 in 2000 to 89,780 in 2016 — a 79% reduction — primarily due to vaccination campaigns. The estimated 21.1 million deaths prevented is widely cited in vaccination advocacy literature.

text: Drinking cold water immediately after a meal causes the fats in your food to solidify in your stomach, leading to cancer and clogged arteries. You should only drink room-temperature or hot water with meals.
explanation: False. The human body maintains a constant internal temperature regardless of ingested food or liquid temperatures. Dietary fats are not absorbed from the stomach — they are processed in the small intestine where temperature is constant. Cold water does not solidify fat or cause cancer.

text: The World Health Organization defines 'One Health' as an integrated approach recognizing that the health of humans, animals, and the environment are closely interconnected and interdependent.
explanation: Accurate. The 'One Health' concept is formally endorsed by WHO, FAO, UNEP, and WOAH. It recognizes that 75% of emerging infectious diseases originate in animals, and that antibiotic resistance, food safety, and environmental health all require coordinated human-animal-ecosystem approaches.

text: Ayurvedic heavy metal medicines ('Rasa shastra') containing lead, mercury, and arsenic have been documented to cause severe poisoning in patients. Several product lines sold in the U.S. and India contain dangerous levels of these metals.
explanation: Accurate. Multiple peer-reviewed studies and FDA analyses found commercially available Ayurvedic preparations with toxic heavy metal concentrations. A 2008 JAMA study found 20% of U.S.-manufactured and 21% of Indian-manufactured Ayurvedic products contained detectable lead, mercury, or arsenic.

text: Eating spinach every day will make you as strong as Popeye because spinach contains extremely high levels of iron — more than any other food. Just two cups gives you your entire week's iron requirement.
explanation: False. Spinach does contain iron, but it is non-heme (plant-based) iron with poor bioavailability (~2–8% absorbed vs. 15–35% for heme iron in meat). Additionally, spinach's oxalates inhibit iron absorption further. The Popeye myth originated from a misplaced decimal point in 1800s data that overstated spinach's iron content.

text: The HPV vaccine does not encourage sexual activity in adolescents. Multiple large studies have found no difference in rates of sexual initiation or STI diagnoses between vaccinated and unvaccinated teens.
explanation: Accurate. A common objection to HPV vaccination is that it might promote earlier sexual activity. Multiple large studies — including Canadian studies of hundreds of thousands of girls — found no increase in sexual activity, pregnancy, or other STI rates in vaccinated vs. unvaccinated adolescents.

text: All calories are completely equal regardless of their source — 100 calories from broccoli and 100 calories from sugar have identical effects on your body, metabolism, hormones, and long-term health outcomes.
explanation: False. While total calorie balance matters for weight, the source of calories affects satiety hormones, gut microbiome, blood sugar response, insulin secretion, liver metabolism, and cardiovascular risk. 100 calories of fiber-rich broccoli has profoundly different metabolic effects than 100 calories of fructose.

text: Resistance training (weightlifting) preserves muscle mass and bone density as people age. Adults who strength train regularly have significantly lower rates of osteoporosis, sarcopenia, falls, and fractures.
explanation: Accurate. The American College of Sports Medicine recommends resistance training 2–3 times per week for all adults. Multiple meta-analyses show strength training increases bone mineral density, preserves muscle mass (sarcopenia prevention), improves balance, and reduces fall risk in older adults.

text: Hospitals give patients unnecessary surgeries all the time because surgeons are paid per procedure. Studies show that 90% of all appendectomies, knee surgeries, and tonsillectomies are unnecessary and driven purely by profit.
explanation: False. While overuse of some procedures is a legitimate concern in healthcare, the '90% unnecessary' claim is fabricated. Appendectomy is emergency surgery for life-threatening infection. Studies on some elective procedures do show geographic variation in rates, but nothing near 90% unnecessary across these categories.

text: Skin cancer is the most common cancer in the United States, with approximately 9,500 people diagnosed every day. Melanoma is the deadliest form, responsible for 75% of skin cancer deaths despite being only 5% of cases.
explanation: Accurate. The American Academy of Dermatology reports ~9,500 skin cancer diagnoses daily. Melanoma accounts for only 5% of skin cancers but causes approximately 75% of skin cancer deaths due to its high metastatic potential. UV exposure from sunlight and tanning beds is the primary risk factor.

text: The appendix is a useless vestigial organ with no function. Removing it has absolutely no health consequences, and many surgeons recommend elective appendectomy for everyone over 40 to prevent emergency surgery later.
explanation: False. The appendix contains lymphoid tissue and may function in gut microbiome recolonization after infection. No mainstream surgical guidelines recommend elective appendectomy in healthy adults. While appendectomy is safe, claiming it has 'zero health consequences' ignores surgical risks and the organ's potential immune functions.

text: Sickle cell trait (carrying one copy of the sickle cell gene) provides partial protection against severe malaria, which explains why the sickle cell mutation is most prevalent in populations with ancestral exposure to malaria.
explanation: Accurate. Carriers of one HbS allele have 40–50% reduced risk of severe malaria. This heterozygote advantage explains why sickle cell trait reached high frequencies in sub-Saharan Africa, the Mediterranean, and Middle East — regions historically endemic for malaria. This is a classic example of balancing selection.

text: Cryotherapy chambers that cool your body to -100°C (-148°F) permanently repair cellular DNA damage, reverse aging by 15 years, and cure arthritis, depression, and multiple sclerosis with just three sessions.
explanation: False. Whole-body cryotherapy has limited evidence for modest benefits in muscle recovery after intense exercise. Claims that it reverses aging, repairs DNA, or cures autoimmune diseases are not supported by peer-reviewed evidence. The FDA has warned against unproven cryotherapy health claims.

text: Preterm birth — delivery before 37 weeks of gestation — is the leading cause of death in children under 5 globally and can cause lifelong developmental complications including cerebral palsy, hearing loss, and learning disabilities.
explanation: Accurate. WHO and UNICEF data confirm preterm birth as the leading cause of under-5 mortality worldwide (~1 million deaths annually). Survivors face elevated risks of neurodevelopmental impairment. Risk factors include multiple pregnancy, maternal infections, chronic disease, and poverty.

text: Ivermectin, hydroxychloroquine, and zinc together form a protocol that prevents COVID-19 with 100% effectiveness. Doctors who used this Frontline COVID-19 Critical Care protocol had zero patient deaths, proving vaccines were never needed.
explanation: False. Multiple large randomized controlled trials (RECOVERY, TOGETHER, ACTIV-6, PRINCIPLE) found hydroxychloroquine and ivermectin ineffective against COVID-19. The 'zero deaths' claims from anecdotal early pandemic reports are confounded by selection bias, patient age, and disease severity differences.
